Title: HEPCloud Operations at Fermilab—The First Five Years
Text:
HEPCloud Operations at Fermilab—The First 
Five Years 
Steven Timm1*, Kyle  Knoepfel1, and Nick Smith1 
1Fermilab, P.O. Box 500, Batavia, IL 60510 USA 
Abstract. The HEPCloud Facility at Fermilab has now been in production 
operation for five years. This facility is a unified provisioning gateway to 
US high performance computing centers, including NERSC, OLCF, and 
ALCF, other large supercomputers run by the NSF, and commercial clouds. 
HEPCloud delivers hundreds of millions of core-hours yearly for CMS. 
HEPCloud also serves other Fermilab experiments including DUNE, Mu2e, 
Muon g-2, and NOvA. In this paper we present the practical considerations 
of operating a distributed facility such as HEPCloud. We also mention some 
of the interesting research and development that HEPCloud has been used 
for including GPU-based machine learning inference servers, and tests of 
Quantum Computing.  
1 Introduction 
 
In 2014 the Fermilab Scientific Computing leadership initiated a program of work to 
develop the “Virtual Facility” with the goal of extending our computing resources into 
commercial clouds and HPC resources in addition to the grid computing sites that were 
already in use.  The idea received strong support from experimental stakeholders, 
developers, and funding agencies.  The project received the name “HEPCloud” from Jim 
Siegrist, then the head of the DOE Office of High Energy Physics.   
Some proof-of-principle tests with Amazon Web Services and other commercial 
clouds had already been done[1], as well as some basic tests at  the National Energy 
Resource Scientific Computing Center (NERSC) in Berkeley, CA.  In 2016 two large-scale 
demonstrations were done, one with 60,000 cores on Amazon Web Services[2] and a 
second one with 160,000 on the Google Compute Platform.  Both of these were made 
possible due to grants of computing cycles from those respective companies. 
Panagiotis Spentzouris, then the head of the Scientific Computing Division at 
Fermilab, gave the mandate to build a system that could do all the activities of data-
intensive high-throughput computing, and do it on grid, cloud, or HPC center, with the 
Fermilab facility being in control of where the jobs would run[3]. The system would build

2 Development 
 
The large-scale commercial cloud demonstrations clearly identified several 
components that were needed in the production system.  We needed to control who was 
allowed to run on the cloud and HPC, how much they were allowed to spend, how to 
detect unauthorized use, how to optimize the selection of resources, and how to protect 
all the very valuable secrets that are used to access the various cloud resources. 
The Decision Engine emerged as the solution to both decide what resources ought to 
be requested, and the method to request them.  After an extended time of requirements 
gathering, a large number of developers were assembled to do a code sprint and write the 
basic framework that became the Decision Engine[5].  The key algorithm within the 
Decision Engine is the Figure of Merit.  It ranks all resources by price/performance.  Note 
that cloud resources have dynamic pricing when using spot price instances, so these 
figures of merit are calculated in real time.  The price/performance has units of money, 
and lower is better.   
The decision engine gathers information from external resources by means of Sources.  
These include things such as a list of all remote resources which are available, the 
price/performance of those resources, the total billed amount to date, and the amount of 
jobs from each user that are currently idle. 
Calculations on the raw numbers are done by Transforms, which make calculations 
of the figures of merit above, and then how many compute slots to request from each 
resource, inversely proportional to the figure of merits of each. 
The decisions on which resources to send to are made by a rule-based Logic Engine. 
The Logic Engine controls how many commercial resources can be used at once, and also 
tracks the total expenditure to date and stops submissions if the total is over the budgeted 
limit.   
 
Finally, all requests are made to outside resources by means of Publishers and the 
monitoring is also fed by Publishers. Data is passed between the various sources, 
transforms, and publishers by means of a backend database, in which all the information 
is stored as PanDAS data frames. 
 
After the initial code sprint which produced the first framework, continued 
development continued for two more years on the sources, transforms, and publishers 
that would be necessary to do the full  HEPCloud facility with all the resources unified.  
Two major rewrites of the framework have been done since we initially went to 
production as well.  The most significant changes were re-writing the Logic Engine in 
python rather than C++, and redoing the database backend such that the output from 
sources is cached in memory using the Redis in-memory database and only written to the 
Postgres database at the end of the decision cycle.

3.1 Initial Deployment  
In March 2019 the HEPCloud deployment was declared to be production.  In its initial 
configuration it queried job queues and could send jobs to any of AWS, Google, NERSC, 
OSG, and local clusters simultaneously.  Note that when we refer to “sending jobs” what 
we are in fact doing is submitting pilot jobs, or pilot VM calls, to the remote resource and 
those jobs call back to our unified resource pool.  Thanks to late binding we do not get 
jobs stuck waiting for a resource that we think may come available, we can run the jobs 
on the first resource that is available.    
The first big user was USCMS, who had been running jobs at NERSC via our 
integration instance for more than a year.  CMS added a requirement that they wanted 
to control which jobs went to cloud and HPC resources.  They prioritized jobs for HPC 
where the right inputs such as pile-up files were available, and the duration and memory 
footprint of the jobs were appropriate for finishing on those resources.  The configuration 
that was agreed to and has persisted to the present day, was that the CMS production staff 
would tag jobs which were eligible for running on HEPCloud, either  on supercomputing 
sites or on the commercial cloud.  The CMS Global pool uses condor flocking to send jobs 
to HEPCloud and we request remote resources based on the number of idle jobs.  Other 
stakeholders from Fermilab fixed-target and neutrino experiments, do the same with 
their grid cluster and only tag the jobs available for the HPC clusters. Within the last two 
years DUNE has also established its own Global Pool with its own decision engine. 
The initial NERSC machine we ran on was Edison, followed by Cori which was 
dominantly the many-core Intel “Knight’s Landing” architecture, Xeon Phi™ Processor 
7250 nodes @1.4 GHz with 68 cores. We added a correction factor to the provisioning to 
allow for the longer execution time on this platform so we did not assign jobs that could 
not finish in the allotted time.  Cori was replaced by NERSC Perlmutter. Perlmutter 
consists of 1536 GPU accelerated nodes with 1 AMD Milan processor and 4 NVIDIA A100 
GPUs, and 3072 CPU-only nodes with 2 AMD Milan processors. Given the way that the 
SLURM priorities work at NERSC, with just two jobs getting incremented in priority at 
any one time, we have at various times found it useful to submit pilot jobs with up to 100 
nodes starting simultaneously.  NERSC gives the option to run the same pilot job on all 
100 nodes without having to use MPI to launch it. 
 
3.2 Expansion to XSEDE (ACCESS) 
  
USCMS received allocations on the National Science Foundation(NSF) XSEDE 
(eXtreme Science and Engineering Discovery Environment) system[6], later known as 
ACCESS (Advanced Cyberinfrastructure Coordination Ecosystem: Services and Support).  
These resources are x86_64 based architecture and good sources of computing cycles.  
Initially we onboarded at Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center, their Bridges machine and 
later their Bridges2 machine.  We shortly added Stampede2 at the Texas Advanced 
Computing Center (TACC).  We also received allocations on Frontera at TACC even 
though this machine is not part of XSEDE.  The Stampede3 computer at TACC was just 
recently made available and we are working on onboarding it now. At the San Diego

Finally at the Rosen Center for Advanced Computing (RCAC) at Purdue we got

front of an MS Azure allocation for a one-time availability of MS Azure cycles. 
The hosted-CE is an important tool in making these NSF-based computers easily 
accessible.  As far as HEPCloud is concerned it appears to be just another grid site. The 
hosted-CE for HPC sites are managed by OSG staff on behalf of USCMS and hosted on 
OSG Kubernetes infrastructure. 
 
3.3 Batch Submission Protocols 
The HTCondor developers have been very helpful over the years in adding all the 
various new submission protocols to HTCondor so that we can submit to all the different 
resources we deal with.  Amazon Web Services uses the “EC2” (Elastic Compute Cloud) 
protocol.  Google Compute Platform uses a google API.  NERSC uses the htcondor “batch 
universe” which was originally known as BOSCO.  This handles job submission and file 
transfer over an ssh connection to the remote machine.  At submit time it accesses the 
remote host and runs a set of scripts to submit the job, and then there is another set of 
polling scripts.  It can also forward updated credentials to the job as needed.   NERSC 
introduced Multi Factor Authentication to their login system a few years ago, but it is 
still possible to do passwordless/MFA login via credentials they refer to as the “sshproxy”.  
This is a PKCS-8 signed private ssh key which has a validity of one month before it must 
be renewed.  NERSC also introduced the “Superfacility API” which we are using to 
update our usage and quota information, but not yet for submission of jobs. 
3.4 Data Transfer 
 
Most CMS jobs that run on HEPCloud are step-chain workflows which run the whole 
Monte Carlo chain from event generation to digitization and reconstruction.  These jobs 
all need pile-up files and CMS has what’s called “pre-mix” pileup.  In the early days we 
transferred a full dataset of pile-up to NERSC scratch. Now it is read across the network 
from Fermilab.  The output files that are produced are staged out directly to Fermilab. 
DUNE and other neutrino experiments stage local flux files and photon shower 
libraries on the Community File System at NERSC.  The files have historically been 
output to Perlmutter Scratch system and transported back to Fermilab via FTS3.  A Rucio 
storage element is currently being commissioned by DUNE at NERSC. 
3.5 Code distribution 
The physics code of the various experiments that HEPCloud deals with is all available in 
CVMFS, which is an http-based file system.  On the commercial clouds we controlled the

virtual machine and thus could start up cvmfs clients and squid servers as necessary.  CMS 
also gets their conditions database distributed over the net via the Frontier system.   
On the high performance computing systems, initially most of them did not have a 
working /cvmfs system, and if they did they were syncing the contents of /cvmfs to a 
local file system and then exporting it over the network.   At NERSC CMS first tried to 
launch a container using their “shifter” system which contained all the CMS code.  The 
jobs were unable to start because the container was too big and thus NERSC agreed to put 
in at first a network-synced CVMFS system and then later a native CVMFS client system. 
Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center also installed a network-synced CVMFS client 
system as did SDSC.  At TACC we use a product called “cvmfsexec” which runs in user 
space on each worker node and handles the work necessary to fetch the files from the 
CVMFS server into a user area which is then bind-mounted to the container in which 
the job runs.  It is necessary to have user namespaces enabled in the kernel for this to 
work, but all of these sites have that. 
It should be noted that CVMFS is also used to export a set of images for the OS 
environment in which the job runs. These are images for Apptainer (formerly known as 
singularity) and it allows for running a workflow of heterogeneous jobs that require 
different operating systems, all in the same cluster.   NERSC uses the “Shifter” container 
system for this purpose.  
 
3.6 I/O challenges 
 
The shared file systems at HPC centers are often based on Lustre and don’t handle 
some HEP applications well.  HEP jobs such as Madgraph use large numbers of inodes 
and a heavy input/output rate. In addition, the compute nodes of HPC often have little 
to no local disk, such that we sometimes see all the disk space allocated on a node before 
we run out of either CPUs or ram. 
At NERSC we are using the “Node Cache” which mounts a share of the flash-based 
Perlmutter scratch as a block device and makes it available to the local worker node.  This 
has proved to be quite performant but only works with the Shifter container system. 
In early work on high performance computing machines we discovered that even if 
there was connectivity to the outside world, the transition between the high-
performance internal network fabric of the cluster and the WAN could sometimes be 
dropped.   This was most often at the output stage. For different stakeholders we worked 
around this by staging output files at the local storage of the HPC, or by setting up by 
retrying the transfers. We also exceeded the rate limitations of some of the site firewalls.  
This was mitigated by the site putting a hard limit on the number of jobs we could run 
simultaneously. 
3.7 Current deployment challenges 
HEPCloud has strong incentive from our various experimental stakeholders as well as 
their funding agencies to make use of the leadership-class facilities at Argonne and Oak 
Ridge.  These machines, like their predecessors, have no inbound or outbound

connections to the Internet.  They are thus not compatible with the standard 
GlideinWMS pilot job model on which all of our stakeholders rely.  A number of 
demonstrations have been done so far of what is referred to as the “split starter” technique 
in HTCondor.  Part of the condor_starter process runs on an edge node and the rest of it 
runs on the batch node.  They use the shared file system to communicate. These 
demonstrations have been successful at the order of a few thousand jobs, but more work 
is needed to harden the technique, due to some fraction of jobs failing to finish.  In the 
time since we did these demonstrators, the staff of the Barcelona Supercomputing Center 
have successfully run this same technique (which they initially helped to develop) with 
an order of magnitude more cores than we have[7].   
  We are in conversation with all of the leadership-class facilities currently, and 
planning for the era of the Integrated Research Infrastructure.  DUNE in particular has 
part of its near detector reconstruction that uses machine learning[8] which can only be 
done on GPU and may require as many as O(106) GPU node-hours to process the 
reconstruction and simulation of the DUNE near detector for one year of running, 
assuming performance of current Perlmutter GPU hardware. 
4 Novel Commercial Cloud Uses 
HEPCloud has found that the best efficiency of commercial cloud usage is for special 
purpose hardware which would be too expensive to acquire and maintain on a full time 
basis, or that would become obsolete too quickly.   Within the Sonic project we have 
done several large-scale tests of nVIDIA Triton Inference Server on commercial clouds.  
These include testing tensor processors and FPGA-based servers as the machines on 
which it runs.  They are optimized for applications in which the GPU or other exotic 
hardware is only called out for a relatively short duration of the full job, usually at the 
end.  Typically the system is configured to have O(1000) worker node jobs call out to a 
single inference server[9].   
We have done tests where workers and inference server are both in the cloud, and 
other tests where we used workers at Fermilab to call out to the inference server in 
Google cloud (Iowa availability zone).  In one such test we managed to use up the entire 
off-site network bandwidth of Fermilab[10]. 
Our efforts are now to co-schedule an inference server job on NERSC Perlmutter, 
scheduling the inference server and the rest of the job simultaneously with both CPUs 
and GPUs in the resources of the job. 
We also used Amazon Web Services in an evaluation project to connect to the Rigetti 
corporation quantum computer, since their gateway to it was hosted there, and 
successfully submitted some quantum computing applications through the HEPCloud 
mechanism to run in an AWS VM and call out to the quantum computer for the quantum 
phase.

The overall usage of HEPCloud from October 2020 until October of 2024 is shown in 
Figure 1 for USCMS and Figure 2 for all other projects.  The plots show the total number 
of CPUs that were claimed by HEPCloud jobs at any given time.   A straight average of 
Figure 1 shows that we averaged 26729 cores DC over the four-year period that is plotted.  
There were several peaks of greater than 100,000 cores during that time.  During periods 
of stable operation and sufficient workflow, HEPCloud regularly delivers an amount of 
computing roughly equal to all the resources that are at the USCMS Tier 1 facility at 
Fermilab. HEPCloud has also been used by the NOvA, Mu2e, Muon g-2, DUNE, 
MicroBoone, and ICARUS experiments at Fermilab thus far. 
6 Conclusions 
HEPCloud is now a mature provisioning system which provides access to compute 
resources of size comparable to the CMS Tier-1 facility at Fermilab.  Over the last six 
years we have been able to grow the capacity thanks to increasing allocations from the 
DOE ERCAP program and the NSF ACCESS CI program.  HEPCloud has shown to be a
